summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive 3D web app that helps mission planners, educators and the public choose where and when to land near the Moon's south pole. There the Sun skims the horizon and Earth bobs above and below it, so the local hills decide whether a lander gets sunlight for power and a direct radio link home. Pick a site, or click anywhere on the Moon: the app combines NASA JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions with the real skyline from NASA LRO LOLA terrain. It shows when each is visible, time to sunset and Earthset, the share of the year with both, and the best landing windows, and it compares sites side by side. Every number comes from traceable physics, not machine learning, and is cross-checked against NASA illumination maps and Apollo records. A 3D-printed tabletop model of the Shackleton rim shows the same horizon physically. It turns NASA tools that are hard for non-experts into fast, visual answers.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator helps mission planners, educators and the public choose where and when to land at the Moon's south pole. There the Sun skims the horizon and Earth bobs above and below it, so the local hills decide the two things a lander needs: sunlight for solar power and a direct radio line to Earth.

How it works. Pick one of 39 sites (south-pole candidates, north-pole sites and past landings), or click anywhere on a 3D Moon. For that spot we ask NASA JPL Horizons where the Sun and Earth appear to an observer standing on the Moon, every hour for 30 days and every 6 hours for a year. We then compare that with the real local skyline, built from NASA LRO LOLA terrain. The app shows whether the Sun and Earth are up right now, the time to sunset and Earthset, the share of the year with sunlight, Earth in view and both together, the longest stretch with both, the longest dark stretch, and the best 7, 14 or 30-day landing windows. You can compare two sites or two moments side by side. A horizon strip and the 3D sky show the Sun and Earth against the real hills as you move through time. For example, at the Shackleton crater rim the Sun is up 78.2% of the year, Earth 50.0%, and both 40.2%.

Why trust it. There's no machine learning: every number comes from physics and geometry on NASA data and can be traced. We checked our results against NASA GSFC polar illumination and Earth-visibility maps at 13 polar sites (mean difference about 2 percentage points), against the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal's Sun angles (mean 0.08°), against LROC stereo terrain at all 6 Apollo sites, and with 112 physics checks. The app states its limits openly, for example that landing within about 60 m matters near the pole.

Creativity. A tabletop companion model: a 3D-printed Shackleton-rim horizon made from the same LOLA skyline turns on a stepper motor under a lamp (the Sun), with a servo-driven Earth, all driven from the app by an Arduino UNO Q. The software works fully without the hardware.

Tools. Python (NumPy, Flask), JavaScript (three.js, Vite), Arduino UNO Q, SolidWorks, a Bambu Lab 3D printer, and AWS (EC2, CloudFront, S3) for hosting. Claude (Anthropic) was used as an AI coding assistant.

What we considered. Traceable, cross-checked numbers; plain-language explanations ("i" buttons) for non-experts; and working offline for live demos.
dataRefs: NASA JPL Horizons System (Sun and Earth positions seen from the lunar surface)
LRO LOLA Gridded Data Records (lunar terrain LDEM_128, polar DEMs)
NASA GSFC PGDA Lunar Polar Illumination and Earth Visibility Maps (Mazarico et al. 2011)
LRO LROC NAC Digital Terrain Models, Apollo sites
NASA Moon Trek (Moon imagery tiles, landing-site coordinates)
projectRefs: USGS / IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature (lunar feature names)
Apollo Lunar Surface Journal (Sun and Earth angles for accuracy checks)
Wikipedia: List of artificial objects on the Moon (past landing coordinates)
Amazon Web Services (EC2, CloudFront and S3 hosting)
